text: The applicant was born in 1972.
The applicant lives in Kharkiv.
The applicant was represented by Mr Y. Borysenko, a lawyer practising in Kharkiv.
The Government were represented by their acting Agent, Ms O. Davydchuk, of the Ministry of Justice.
The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.
On 11 August 2012 the applicant informed the local police in Kharkiv of his intention to hold a peaceful assembly under the banner of 'Ukraine for fair elections'.
The applicant's intended assembly was planned to run from 12 August 2012 onwards for an indefinite period of time.
The applicant's intended assembly was planned to be held in Shevchenko Park in Kharkiv city centre.
The local police in Kharkiv transmitted the applicant's notice of intended assembly to the Kharkiv City Council.
There is no information as to whether the applicant actually attempted to hold the demonstration on 12 August 2012 as he declared to the authorities.
On 13 August 2012 the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council decided that the assembly that the applicant planned to hold should not be permitted.
On 13 August 2012 the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council requested the local court to prohibit the applicant's planned assembly.
On 13 August 2012 the Kharkiv District Administrative Court allowed the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council's request and prohibited the applicant's planned assembly.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the matters under examination were regulated by the Temporary Regulations on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Kharkiv.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the Temporary Regulations on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Kharkiv were binding under section 73 of the Local Self-Government in Ukraine Act.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the procedure set out in the Temporary Regulations on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Kharkiv for the examination by the local authorities of the applicant's notification had been observed.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the notice sent by the applicant did not provide clear details of the assembly.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the notice had not been sent a reasonable time in advance, noting that it was dated 11 August 2012 and had been received by the Kharkiv City Council on 13 August 2012, whereas the assembly had been scheduled for 12 August 2012.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the applicant planned to hold an assembly for an indefinite period of time.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the applicant had chosen the city centre as the location for the assembly, not far from areas with significant levels of road traffic.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the proposed location of the assembly was a place where the people of Kharkiv liked to rest and take part in leisure activities.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that 'there was no evidence to prove that the assembly was not contrary to the interests of the inhabitants of Kharkiv'.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the assembly could pose a risk to the health and life of the inhabitants of Kharkiv, as well as their right to move about safely in the city.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court stated that 'the material in the case file [did] not demonstrate that there [was] no possibility of a violation of the rights and freedoms of people [not participating in the assembly]'.
On 17 September 2012 the Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the prohibition of the planned assembly.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the time and place of the applicant's planned assembly coincided with the time and place of the Honey Fair and the Flower Show, which were to take place from 14 to 23 August 2012 in Shevchenko Park.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the holding of the applicant's assembly at the same time and place as the Honey Fair and the Flower Show could lead to a breach of public order and a threat to safety, because the applicant's assembly could spontaneously be joined by an unknown number of people.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that if the applicant's assembly were spontaneously joined by additional people, the number of participants would increase and the assembly would become unmanageable, all of which would hinder the movement of people and vehicles.
On 15 November 2012 the Higher Administrative Court rejected a request by the applicant for leave to appeal on points of law.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that citizens have the right to assemble peacefully without arms and to hold meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations, after notifying the executive authorities and bodies of local self-government beforehand.

text: Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that restrictions on the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly may be established by a court in accordance with the law, in the interests of national security and public order only, for the purpose of preventing disturbances or crimes, protecting the health of the population, or protecting the rights and freedoms of other persons.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 92 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that human and citizens' rights and freedoms, the guarantees of these rights and freedoms, and the main duties of the citizen shall be determined exclusively by the laws of Ukraine.

text: In its decision of 19 April 2001 in a case regarding the timely notification of a peaceful assembly, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine noted that the Ministry of the Interior of Ukraine had applied to the Constitutional Court of Ukraine for an official interpretation of the provisions of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine regarding timely notification to executive authorities or bodies of local self-government of planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
E. Decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001

text: In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine noted that the current legislation of Ukraine does not provide for a specific time-limit within which the executive authorities or bodies of local self-government are to be notified about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
E. Decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001

text: In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the provisions of the first part of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine on timely notification to the executive authorities or bodies of local self-government of planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations shall be understood to mean that where the organisers of such peaceful gatherings are planning to hold such an event, they must inform the above-mentioned authorities in advance, that is, within a reasonable time prior to the date of the planned event.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
E. Decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001

text: In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the time-limits for notification should not restrict the right of citizens under Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, but should serve as a guarantee of this right and at the same time should provide the relevant executive authorities or bodies of local self-government with an opportunity to take measures to ensure that citizens may freely hold meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations and to protect public order and the rights and freedoms of others.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
E. Decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001

text: In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that specifying the exact deadlines for timely notification with regard to the particularities of different forms of peaceful assembly, the number of participants, the venue, and the time of the event is a matter for legislative regulation.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
E. Decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001

text: On 20 December 2012 the United Nations Human Rights Council published the Report of the Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review in respect of Ukraine (UN Doc. A/HRC/22/7).
section_path: A. United Nations Human Rights Council

text: In the Report of the Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review in respect of Ukraine (UN Doc. A/HRC/22/7), one of the recommendations made to Ukraine was to implement a law on freedom of assembly that complies with applicable standards under Article 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which recognises the right of peaceful assembly.
section_path: A. United Nations Human Rights Council

text: In its Resolution 2116 (2016) on the urgent need to prevent human rights violations during peaceful protests, dated 27 May 2016, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe noted that it was worried about the lack of legislation on freedom of assembly in certain countries, including Ukraine, where there is no legislation with respect to a procedure for holding demonstrations.
section_path: B. Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe

text: Between 2006 and 2011 the European Commission for Democracy through Law (Venice Commission), together with the Office for Democratic Institution and Human Rights of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE/ODIHR), issued four joint opinions on the draft legislation of Ukraine on freedom of assembly.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: None of the draft laws on freedom of assembly submitted to the Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR for assessment between 2006 and 2011 was eventually passed.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: In October 2016 the Venice Commission adopted a Joint Opinion with the Directorate of Human Rights of the Directorate General of Human Rights and Rule of Law of the Council of Europe and the OSCE/ODIHR on two draft laws of Ukraine on guarantees for freedom of peaceful assembly (no. 854/2016).
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that the Venice Commission, the Directorate of Human Rights of the Directorate General of Human Rights and Rule of Law of the Council of Europe, and the OSCE/ODIHR delegation learned during their most recent visit in Kyiv that civil society appeared to be divided on the need to adopt specific legislation on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that supporters of the 'no-law approach' claimed that civil society in Ukraine is still too weak to control the Verkhovna Rada and feared that if specific legislation were adopted, the Verkhovna Rada could introduce negative amendments into the specific law during possible future political crises.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that supporters of the 'no-law approach' considered that a safer method would be to amend the existing legislation in order to introduce regulations on freedom of assembly and to adopt some secondary legislation in this field.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that others asserted that the adoption of a specific law on public assemblies would provide greater clarity and precision regarding the obligations of the State in this field, the grounds for restriction, and the procedures to be followed.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that in the absence of clear legislative regulations on freedom of assembly, local authorities in Ukraine have issued specific and widely varying local rules in order to regulate the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR

text: The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that according to certain civil society organisations, regulation of the right to freedom of assembly by local decisions is a widespread practice in Ukraine, which would contradict Article 92 of the Constitution of Ukraine, which provides that human and citizens' rights and freedoms are determined exclusively by the laws of Ukraine.
section_path: C. The Venice Commission and the OSCE/ODIHR
